Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF). Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute
Additional Titles
The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative
Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative
Summary
Proposition 38 began as a citizen-initiated state statute filed with the California Attorney General’s Office (https://oag.ca.gov/) who cleared the initiative for signature gathering on January 2, 2026. To qualify for the ballot, proponents were required to collect 546,651 valid signatures. On June 23, 2026, the Secretary of State announced that the campaign collected enough signatures that the initiative qualified for the November 2026 ballot as Proposition 38.
Proposition 38 authorizes California to issue an $8.4 billion general obligation bond to fund medical research in immunology and immunotherapy, with state payments taken from the state General Fund. The measure mandates that at least $4.2 billion be dedicated specifically to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease, while capping state administrative expenditures at 2 percent. The bond proceeds are divided equally between a designated specialized research institute selected by the California Department of Public Health (https://www.cdph.ca.gov/) that meets specific size, funding, and University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/) (UC) collaboration criteria, while the remaining half is distributed as competitive research grants to California universities and non-profit research institutions via an advisory council.
Proposition 38 mandates that the institute generate as much revenue as possible from the funded research. Ten percent of this revenue would go to the state’s General Fund until the research bond is repaid. Additional funding would be used for future immunotherapy and immunology research. Grant recipients are required to purchase at least half of their goods and services from California suppliers whenever feasible, and any treatments developed through this research and sold within California must generally be offered to patients at a 20 percent discount. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements. Both the designated institute and the grant council are subject to annual public reporting and independent financial audit requirements.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
If Proposition 38 passes, the state General Fund would incur an estimated annual repayment cost of $500 million to $600 million over roughly 20 years to pay off the bond. This would amount to about 0.25% of the state's total General Fund budget and approximately 10% more total cost (adjusted for inflation) than upfront funding due to interest. Offsetting these expenditures, the state could potentially earn significant revenue from commercialized research treatments funded by the measure, though the amount and timing remain uncertain and could take decades to materialize. Additionally, the initiative would generate indirect fiscal effects on state health programs like Medi-Cal, where net costs could rise or fall depending on the pricing and adoption of newly developed medical treatments.
What your vote means
YES: A YES vote supports issuing $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, allocating half of the funds to a University of California-affiliated research institute and distributing the remainder as grants to California public and nonprofit medical research institutions.
NO: A NO vote opposes issuing $8.4 billion in state bonds to fund immunology and immunotherapy research and treatment development.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents believe that The California Immunology Research & Cures Initiative aims to accelerate lifesaving medical breakthroughs by investing in immunotherapies that empower the patient's own immune system to target and combat disease. Supporters emphasize that because these therapies are already effectively treating certain cancers and chronic conditions, dedicated state funding will help move proven, cutting-edge science out of the research lab and into clinical treatments for patients more quickly.
The opposition argues that Proposition 38 is a deceptive measure designed to benefit its billionaire donor by funneling state resources toward a single institution using arbitrary criteria. Opponents contend that state funds for medical research should instead be allocated through a fair, competitive process where all eligible applicants have an equal opportunity to compete.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It’s easy to see why Newsom’s support is flying under the radar. At first glance, voting for Prop 38 seems like a no-brainer. Who wouldn’t support funding medical research into potential treatments and cures for diseases like cancer and Alzheimer’s? It’s no surprise that polls show 57% of voters (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) supporting it.
But you are being deceived.
The measure is a Trojan horse that would funnel billions of taxpayer dollars into an untested pet project founded by the same group of billionaires that paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot.
“Shady” doesn’t even begin to describe it.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 38 would permit the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy, scientific fields that examine how the body’s immune system can be harnessed to fight disease. Californians would get a 20% discount on drugs that receive commercial approval, with 10% of revenue flowing back to the state.
So far, so good.
That was until the online news site CalMatters discovered (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) that the measure stockpiles half the funds — $4.2 billion in taxpayer dollars — for a single unnamed institute that meets a long list of strange requirements (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf), some of which have nothing to do with the ability to conduct high-quality medical research.
Among them: The institute must occupy a minimum 200,000-square-foot space, be linked to a University of California campus healthcare system with more than 35,000 annual inpatient hospital admissions and have received a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
Only one facility in the state meets those criteria: The California Institute of Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
This recently formed institute — which has an opaque affiliation with UCLA but will operate mostly independently — was founded by the same group of billionaires that gathered signatures to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and the Trump-pardoned “junk bond king,” (https://www.cnn.com/2020/02/18/investing/michael-milken-pardon) Michael Milken, who’ve raised nearly $72 million to flood the airwaves with ads touting the measure (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
But it has no track record of doing, well, anything.
It’s not even fully built, despite receiving $250 million in philanthropic money — and an infusion of $200 million in California taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park).
In 2024, Newsom trumpeted that investment (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) as one that would help “cement California’s global economic, scientific, and technological dominance into the 22nd century and beyond.” But an institute spokesperson acknowledged (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php) that construction on a “majority” of its space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028.
The institute doesn’t even have a director. In fact, it only had three employees as of September, despite having planned to hire 51 by last year, CalMatters reported (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTExMDkxfDJmOTZmZWFlYmY4YmQ0NGZkMGFhZTNkYWFlZTQ4NGE1ZmYyY2M4N2M4MDRlZTg1N2U4OTVkMTFjNmNhOGFiN2Q&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=They%20killed%20with%20their%20big%20rigs%20%20The%20DMV%20routinely%20did%20nothing&utm_campaign=WhatMatters).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In other words, it’s nowhere near ready for primetime.
Despite that, Prop 38 also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through research funded by the measure — even those created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
California has some of the top scientific research institutions in the world, yet Prop 38 is poised to hand control of a huge funding pipeline to a partially constructed facility with no one in charge and fewer employees than your local Starbucks.
It isn’t just ridiculous; it’s insulting.
All we’ve heard this election cycle is that the pending Trump administration-supported healthcare cuts by Congress are going to leave California’s most vulnerable residents without care.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Yet the billionaires behind Prop 38 have the audacity to ask California residents to eat decades of debt payments — about $500 million to $600 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop38-110326.pdf) for 20 years — to fund a project they could easily pay for themselves. All while papering over that selfishness by invoking vulnerable patients and suffering families.
And then there’s our governor.
Newsom’s support of Prop 38 is particularly infuriating given that there’s a $7.5 billion scientific research bond (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) headed for the March 2028 ballot. Authorized by a bill from state Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, the measure would create a state foundation to award grants and make loans through a peer-reviewed process to universities, research companies and institutes for biomedical, behavioral health and climate research.
Wiener’s bond better aligns with how scientific research should be funded, said Robert Kaplan, senior scholar at the Stanford School of Medicine Clinical Excellence Research Center and former associate director at the National Institutes of Health.
Money should be competitively awarded, not handed to just one institution or prioritized for just one field of study, Kaplan, a Prop 38 opponent, said. He added that unlike Prop 38, Wiener’s bond “has the kinds of transparency protections that I think taxpayers would expect.”
Newsom made a huge show of signing Wiener’s bill — his final one as governor — in an ostentatious ceremony atop the Golden Gate Bridge (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/newsom-golden-gate-bridge.html).
Yet his backing of Prop 38 risks undermining support for that effort, as voters tend to get confused and fatigued by a surplus of bond measures.
In other words, Newsom is tipping the scales toward a sketchy institute that might not even have a completed building by March 2028 over a far superior effort with the potential to deliver meaningful scientific advances.
Asked for comment, Newsom’s press office referred me to his campaign team, which didn’t respond to multiple inquiries.
That’s not surprising. This is an impossible position to defend.
As someone who suffers from an autoimmune condition (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/weight-lifting-exercise-gym-benefit-22362639.php), I don’t take issue with investing in immunology and immunotherapy research. Far from it.
But I do object to handing a pot of gold to an unproven institute — the lab equivalent of a nepo baby — instead of prioritizing funds for rigorously vetted research projects that show the greatest possibility of making a difference.

And I take issue with Prop 38’s backers cramming their crooked measure onto a crowded ballot, crossing their fingers that voters won’t have time to do their research.
Honestly, Newsom’s willingness to back this deceptive measure is so bad it should be a deal-breaker for anyone considering supporting his likely quest for the Oval Office.

Proposition 38 : $8.4 billion bond for immunology research
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling bonds for research on immunology and immunotherapy, with at least $4.2 billion for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer's disease. About half would go to one research institute tied to a University of California campus, chosen by the Department of Public Health, and half to research grants. Treatments developed with the money would generally have to be sold in California at a 20% discount.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 38 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/).
Results
Polls close at 8 p.m. Pacific on Nov. 3. First results appear here after that.
At a glance
Proposition 38
Borrowing $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds
Repayment $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years from the state General Fund
Split About half to one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute; half to grants chosen by a council of UC and other institutions
Likely institute California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy at the UCLA Research Park, per UCLA and CalMatters
Money raised, Jan. 1, 2025 to Nov. 1, 2026 For: $71.4 million, including $60.2 million in loans. Against: $11,990
Largest funder Gary K. Michelson and his Michelson Center for Public Policy: $66.4 million in gifts and loans
Latest public poll PPIC, Oct. 16-22: 57% yes, 41% no (likely voters)
Each figure is sourced in the sections below. Money figures are our totals from the committees' state campaign reports.
Details and source links: Polls , Money for and against , What it costs , Sources .
What does a yes vote on Proposition 38 mean?
The state could borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
What does a no vote on Proposition 38 mean?
The state could not borrow $8.4 billion to support medical research in immunology and immunotherapy conducted by California research institutes and universities.
What would Proposition 38 cost?
The Legislative Analyst estimates the state would pay $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years to repay the bond, about 0.25% of the state General Fund budget. Ten percent of any revenue from discoveries would go to the state until the bond is repaid. The Analyst says that revenue is uncertain and could take decades.
What it means for the City of LA
Half the money, about $4.2 billion, would go to one institute. UCLA says only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is being built at the UCLA Research Park on the former Westside Pavilion site in Los Angeles, meets the criteria among UCLA's affiliates. Grant recipients would also have to offer UCLA a role in their clinical trials. Bond payments come from the state General Fund; the Legislative Analyst identifies no direct City cost.
The details
Official title Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute.
Type Initiative statute (general obligation bond), placed on the ballot by petition signatures
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide
The question on your ballot
Authorizes $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, half to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute, half to research grants. Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years to repay the research bond, with some or all of the cost offset if the funded research generates revenue. Supporters: Michael J. Fox Foundation; Alzheimer’s Los Angeles; Kidney Cancer Assoc; American Nurses Assoc\CA Opponents: Robert M Kaplan Ph.D.

Who gets the money Not applicable About half to one nonprofit institute chosen by the Department of Public Health. The other half as grants chosen by a council of seven UC campuses and 10 to 15 other California universities and research institutions, from among the council’s own member institutions (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm))
Disease focus Not applicable At least $4.2 billion for cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm))
Institute requirements Not applicable A nonprofit founded for immunology before Jan. 1, 2025; affiliated by then with a UC campus whose health system has more than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3.5 million outpatient visits a year; a research site of at least 200,000 square feet by Jan. 1, 2026; and at least $250 million in philanthropic commitments. If no institute qualifies, the department may loosen the criteria (text, Sec. 130353 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4))
Returns to the state Not applicable Recipients pay the state 10% of revenue from discoveries, first to repay the bond’s full cost. Treatments sold in California must generally carry a 20% discount (Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm))
Oversight Not applicable A six-member Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee chaired by the State Controller, annual reports, independent audits and a 2% cap on state administrative costs (text, Secs. 130359-130362 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=8); Legislative Analyst (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm))
Public records Not applicable The institute “shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law,” including the Public Records Act and the open meeting law (text, Sec. 130363 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=9))
Purchasing Not applicable Grant recipients must try to buy more than half their goods and services from California suppliers (text, Sec. 130357 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6))
What it would mean for Los Angeles
The likely institute is in Los Angeles. CalMatters found that the criteria fit only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, and a UCLA spokesperson confirmed that among UCLA’s nonprofit affiliates only that institute could qualify (CalMatters via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/general/this-ca-proposition-will-send-4-billion-to-a-single-nonprofit-who-s-behind-it/ar-AA298mLd)). The institute is part of the UCLA Research Park, which UCLA bought in the former Westside Pavilion mall, 2 miles south of the Westwood campus. The state intended $500 million for the institute and had allocated $200 million at the time (University of California (https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/ucla-acquires-las-former-westside-pavilion-transform-empty-mall-ucla-research-park)). The Department of Public Health would make the final choice (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/retired-government-analysts-raise-alarm-on-immunology-bond-on-november-ballot/ar-AA2c3iYo)).
UCLA’s role in grants. Every grant agreement must offer UCLA “the opportunity to substantially participate in and collaborate on any clinical trials” and offer the selected institute a role in the research (text, Sec. 130357(d)-(e) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=6)). UCLA’s chancellor appoints one of the seven campus members of the grant council’s executive committee (text, Sec. 130355 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=5)).
Cost. Repayment comes from the state General Fund. The Legislative Analyst identifies no direct local cost, and says effects on state health programs such as Medi-Cal are uncertain (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm)).
Signatures. Los Angeles County supplied 248,653 of the 912,308 raw petition signatures, about 27% (our calculation from the Secretary of State random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/2006-randomsample-06-23-26.pdf)).
We found no City of Los Angeles analysis or position on the measure as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
Jan. 2, 2026: The Attorney General issued the petition’s title and summary. The proponent is Gary K. Michelson (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Feb. 13, 2026: The campaign reported 25% of the signatures needed (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures)).
Late April-early May 2026: Petitions with 912,308 raw signatures were filed with the counties (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/2006-randomsample-06-23-26.pdf)).
June 23, 2026: The random sample projected 619,635 valid signatures, more than 110% of the 546,651 needed, and the measure became eligible (random sample count (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/2006-randomsample-06-23-26.pdf)).
Vote needed. A majority of votes cast statewide (Cal. Const., Art. II, Sec. 10 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2010.&article=II)).
Related past measures. Proposition 71 (2004) created the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine with $3 billion in bonds, and Proposition 14 (2020) added $5.5 billion, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/retired-government-analysts-raise-alarm-on-immunology-bond-on-november-ballot/ar-AA2c3iYo)).
What each side says
In the state voter guide. Arguments are the opinions of their authors and have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency (arguments (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument for, signed by Susan Disney Lord of Alzheimer’s Los Angeles, Eugene P. Brandon of the ALS Association and Dr. Brian Shuch of the Kidney Cancer Association (argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
Cures: immunotherapies “are already curing cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia.”
Federal cuts: the bond offsets “massive federal funding cuts” to research.
Cost: designed to pay for itself “WITH NO NET COST TO THE STATE OR TAXPAYERS” through the 10% revenue share.
Patients: a 20% discount in California.
Safeguards: a 2% administrative cap, public disclosure, audits, and no grants to for-profit companies.
The rebuttal, by Robert M. Kaplan, calls the pay-for-itself claim “speculative” and says research priorities belong in the regular budget (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Argument against, by Robert M. Kaplan (argument against (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/arguments-rebuttals.htm)):
“Ballot-box science”: voters should not pick research topics.
Borrowing: bonds suit roads and schools, not research whose payoff is uncertain.
Revenue: universities rarely commercialize therapies themselves, so returns seldom reach the state treasury.
Discount: companies could favor selling in other states.
Alternative: a state research agency modeled on the National Institutes of Health, as proposed by Sen. Scott Wiener.
The supporters’ rebuttal, signed by cancer survivor Andrew Dale of Santa Monica, Anne M. Holloway of the Michael J. Fox Foundation and Chris Tarver of the American Nurses Association\California, repeats the 10% revenue return and the 20% discount (rebuttal (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/arguments-rebuttals.htm)).
Outside the guide.
Yes campaign spokesperson Claudia Briggs told CalMatters: “We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding. We can’t speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify” (CalMatters via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/general/this-ca-proposition-will-send-4-billion-to-a-single-nonprofit-who-s-behind-it/ar-AA298mLd)).
Yes spokesperson Robin Swanson said the institute “very likely meets the criteria” and that “patients don’t have time to wait for another entity to be created” (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/retired-government-analysts-raise-alarm-on-immunology-bond-on-november-ballot/ar-AA2c3iYo)).
Three retired Legislative Analyst’s Office staff spoke against the measure at a No campaign news conference (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/retired-government-analysts-raise-alarm-on-immunology-bond-on-november-ballot/ar-AA2c3iYo)).
Checking the main factual claims against official records.
Claim Who makes it What official records show
Designed to pay for itself, no net cost Yes campaign The Legislative Analyst estimates $500 million to $600 million a year for about 20 years from the General Fund. Revenue from discoveries “could be significant” but is uncertain and could take decades to offset the cost (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm))
About $500 million a year for about 25 years No campaign The guide’s analysis says $500 million to $600 million for “about 20 years” (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm)). The 25-year figure matches the earlier estimate issued when the petition circulated (Secretary of State, eligible measures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/eligible-statewide-initiative-measures))
Borrowing costs more than paying cash No campaign The Legislative Analyst says the bond’s total cost would be about 10% more, after inflation, than paying up front (analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/analysis.htm))
Half the money goes to one unnamed institute No side, CalMatters The text directs the institute share to “a single nonprofit medical research institute” meeting set criteria (text, Sec. 130353 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=4)). UCLA confirmed only one of its affiliates qualifies (CalMatters via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/general/this-ca-proposition-will-send-4-billion-to-a-single-nonprofit-who-s-behind-it/ar-AA298mLd))
Strong accountability Yes campaign The text creates an oversight committee, audits and reports, and also exempts the institute from public records and open meeting laws (text, Secs. 130361-130363 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf#page=8))
Stem cell bonds returned little Former LAO analyst Dan Carson Carson said the state got about $16 million from stem cell intellectual property against about $6 billion in projected repayment costs, the Sacramento Bee reported (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/retired-government-analysts-raise-alarm-on-immunology-bond-on-november-ballot/ar-AA2c3iYo)). We did not check this against state records

Borrow $8.4 billion for immunology research
Proposition 38 would create an $8.4 billion bond largely to fund research into fighting cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s, plus other diseases that can be treated through immunotherapies.
Half the money would go to a research institute affiliated with the University of California.
The other half would be distributed to select public universities and nonprofits.

### Proposition 38: NO
Proposition 38 would allow the state to borrow $8.4 billion to fund research into treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s and other diseases that can be fought through immunotherapy.
It would also require the drugs developed through this research to be sold at discounted rates.
At face value, this proposition seems reasonable.
However, a deeper look into Prop.
38 shows us that it is rife with issues.
CalMatters found that about 50% of the funding sourced from Prop.
38 is likely to go to the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy — a nonprofit that had three employees as of last month.
It is unclear whether this institute has the capacity to handle billions of dollars.
Further, the writer of the proposition, Gary K. Michelson, is the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy’s primary funder.
While we acknowledge the pressing need for more medical research funding, the glaring problems with Prop.
38 make us hesitant to endorse it.
Vote “no” on Prop.
38.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 43 percent said they would vote yes and 51 percent would vote no. When we asked likely voters which of the 14 state propositions they are most interested in, 14 percent chose one of the five legislative ballot measures (7% Proposition 1; 1% Proposition 2; 2% Proposition 4; 2% Proposition 5; 2% Proposition 43). Eighty-six percent are most interested in one of the nine citizens’ initiatives, with about half expressing the most interest in Proposition 39 (23%; Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) and Proposition 40 (22%; Imposes One-Time Tax). There are partisan divides in interest in Proposition 39 (13% Democrat, 47% Republican, 16% independents) and Proposition 40 (27% Democrats, 13% Republicans, 21% independents). Since the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), the share of those most interested in Proposition 40 has increased (16% to 22%).
Citizens’ Initiatives on the November Ballot
In addition to the five legislative measures, voters are weighing in on nine citizens’ initiatives. Overwhelming majorities of California likely voters say that the voter information guide, which is mailed to voters by the California Secretary of State, is very (40%) or somewhat useful (48%; 12% not too useful). Most are very (26%) or somewhat satisfied (59%) with the information that is available to voters about citizens’ initiatives on the state ballot (14% not satisfied).
After reading the ballot title and label for Proposition 3 (Extending Tax on High Incomes), which would make temporary voter-approved tax rates for individuals earning over $371,000 permanent, a majority of likely voters in the state say they would vote yes; four in ten would vote no. Findings were similar in September 2026 (58% yes, 40% no). Today, most Democrats and independents support Proposition 3, while most Republicans oppose. Likely voters who earn less than $40,000 (77%), are age 18 to 34 (73%), or are renters (69%) are among the most likely to say they would vote yes. Majorities across regions are in support, though Central Valley residents are more divided (51% yes, 48% no).
Proposition 37 (Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Home-Buyers), which would authorize $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible California residents fixed-rate mortgages for newly constructed homes below $1.5 million, is supported by about two in three likely voters (65% yes, 32% no). Support was similar in September (61% yes, 35% no). Majorities of Democrats (80%) and independents (54%) are in support; Republicans are more divided (47% yes, 51% no). Majorities across demographic and regional groups say they would vote yes on Proposition 37, and support declines with rising age and income.
A majority of likely voters (57%) would vote yes on Proposition 38 (Authorizes Bonds For Immunology Medical Research), which would authorize $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds. About four in ten would vote no (41%). The share in support is similar to a month ago (55% yes, September 2026). Today, partisans are divided (70% Democrats, 53% independents, 37% Republicans) and majorities across regions and demographic groups are in support of Proposition 38.
Fewer than half of likely voters in the state would vote yes (41%, 58% no) on Proposition 39 (Prohibits Citizens From Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification) which would invalidate mail ballots that do not have the last four digits of a government-issued identification number written on the envelope and prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. Shares were similar a month ago (43% yes, 55% no). Today, most Republicans would vote yes (82%), most Democrats would vote no (84%), and independents are divided (48% yes, 50% no). Majorities across most demographic groups would vote no, except for likely voters whose highest level of education is a high school diploma, who are more divided (48% yes, 49% no).
Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax), which would impose a 5 percent tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion, is supported by 46 percent of likely voters, while 52 percent would vote no. A slim majority was in support in September (52% yes, 46% no). Today, over six in ten Democrats would vote yes, compared to four in ten independents and about two in ten Republicans. Likely voters who are younger (70% 18 to 34), earn less than $40,000 (64%), are Latino (58%), or reside in Los Angeles (53%) are among the most likely to support this proposition.
Likely voters are divided on Proposition 41 (Prohibits New State Taxes Excluding Revenues from State Spending Limit), which would nullify state taxes enacted after January 1 this year that exempt their revenues from the voter-approved state spending limit and requires audits of programs funded by new special taxes (48% yes, 49% no). Support was similar in September (51% yes, 44% no). Today, most Republicans and independents support Proposition 41, compared to about three in ten Democrats. Support varies across demographic and regional groups.
A slim majority of likely voters would vote yes (51%, 47% no) on Proposition 42 (Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes), which would prohibit new state taxes imposed on the ownership of personal property other than real estate. Support was similar a month ago (54% yes, 43% no). Today, most Republicans and independents would vote yes, while most Democrats would vote no. The share in support varies across demographic and regional groups.
Just a quarter of likely voters would vote yes (25%, 71% no) on Proposition 44 (Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services), which would impose penalties on nonprofit community clinics providing primary care to medically underserved areas and populations that spend less than 90 percent of revenue on program services. A majority was opposed in September (34% yes, 61% no). Today, six in ten or more across partisan, demographic, and regional groups would vote no.
Likely voters are divided (46% yes, 50% no) on Proposition 45 (Modifies Environmental Review), which would amend the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for certain projects by setting deadlines to complete environmental review and resolve lawsuits challenging project approvals. Views were similar a month ago (49% yes, 46% no). A majority of Republicans would vote yes, while a majority of Democrats (54%) and half of independents (50%) would vote no. The shares in support vary across partisan, demographic, and regional groups.
State of the State
Ahead of the November election, about four in ten adults (45%) and likely voters (38%) choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as the most important issue facing people in California today. Fewer choose housing costs and availability (12% adults, 13% likely voters). Cost of living is most likely to be chosen as the state’s top issue across parties, regions, and demographic groups.
When asked about the economic outlook for the next 12 months, most Californians are pessimistic, with three in four adults (77%) and likely voters (79%) expecting bad economic times. Seven in ten Californians have held this view since 2025. Today, two in three or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups are pessimistic.
Californians are also pessimistic about the outlook for the state, with about six in ten or fewer adults (59%) and likely voters (55%) saying the state is heading in the wrong direction. At least half of Californians have said the state is heading in the wrong direction since June 2023 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2023/). About half or more across parties, regions, and demographic groups—except for Democrats (35%)—hold this pessimistic view.
Nearly all Californians view housing costs as a problem in their part of California, with a solid majority seeing them as a big problem (64%) and three in ten saying they are somewhat of a problem (32%). Just 4 percent say housing affordability is not a problem. Across regions, San Francisco Bay Area residents (71%) are the most likely to say housing costs are a big problem, while Central Valley residents (50%) are the least likely (Inland Empire: 68%, Los Angeles: 67%, Orange County/San Diego: 64%). The view that housing affordability is a big problem is widely held by about six in ten or more across parties and demographic groups.
With inflation on the rise again, most Californians continue to feel they are falling behind. Today, about three in four California adults (76%) and likely voters (73%) say their income is not keeping up with inflation, similar to results in February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (71% adults, 67% likely voters). This view is widely held, with seven in ten or more adults across regions and demographic groups saying their income has not kept up. This view is also shared across party lines (74% Democrats, 71% Republicans, 76% independents).
As Governor Newsom approaches the last months of his tenure—and as speculation about his political future swirls—just under half of adults and likely voters approve of his job performance (47% adults, 49% likely voters). Until now, majorities of Californians have approved of the governor since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, about seven in ten Democrats, four in ten independents, and about one in ten Republicans approve of the governor. There are also regional differences: a majority of residents in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles approve, compared to fewer than half in the other regions.
Half or fewer adults and likely voters approve of the state legislature (42% adults, 46% likely voters) and the state legislators representing their assembly and senate districts (43% adults, 48% likely voters). About half of Californians have approved of the legislature since last October (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/), and views of state legislators were similar in May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/). Today, about six in ten Democrats approve of the state legislature and their own legislators, compared to nearly four in ten independents and fewer than one in five Republicans.
When asked about their confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections, six in ten likely voters have a great deal (42%) or quite a lot (21%) of confidence, while nearly four in ten have some confidence (15%) or very little confidence (22%). Seven in ten likely voters (71%)—with partisans divided—think it’s a good thing that a vote-by-mail ballot is mailed to every active registered voter before each election.
State of the Nation
Asked about the most important problem facing the US today, Californians are most likely to choose the economy, unemployment, and jobs (26%), followed by threats to democratic norms (18%) and corruption (14%). Across partisan groups, Democrats are most likely to choose threats to democratic norms (29%), while the economy is the top choice among independents (32%) and Republicans (25%). The economy is the top national issue across most regions and demographic groups.
A record-high share (82%) of California adults say the US is headed in the wrong direction (79% likely voters). Most Democrats (95%) and independents (85%) hold this view, whereas Republicans are divided (51% wrong direction, 48% right direction). Three in four or more across regions and demographic groups say the country is headed in the wrong direction. Californians (82%) are more likely to hold this pessimistic view than adults nationwide (72%), according to an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/ABC-Post-Ipsos%20Trend%20Topline%2010.21.pdf) poll.
Only about three in ten adults say that people who share their political views in the US are extremely (9%) or very (22%) free to express them (likely voters: 11% extremely, 24% very). Conversely, similar shares believe that people who share their political views are a little (16% adults, 14% likely voters) or not at all free (13% adults, 11% likely voters) to openly express them. Three in ten adults and a third of likely voters (36%) believe people who share their views are somewhat free to express them. Views were similar among adults nationwide in a June Pew Research Center (https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/2026/09/15/americans-value-press-freedom-but-differ-on-its-limits/) survey.
Most California adults say freedom of the press is at least somewhat important to the well-being of society (92% adults, 95% likely voters). While majorities across partisan groups share this view, Democrats (68%) are far more likely than independents (49%) and Republicans (27%) to say freedom of the press is extremely important.
When asked about the way democracy is working in the US, just three in ten adults (5% very, 26% somewhat) and likely voters (7% very, 25% somewhat) say they are satisfied. About seven in ten say they are not satisfied with democracy in the US (adults: 39% not too, 29% not at all; likely voters: 37% not too, 31% not at all). About three in four Democrats (79%) and independents (74%) express dissatisfaction, while a majority of Republicans (59%) are satisfied. Six in ten or more across regions and demographic groups are dissatisfied.
About two in ten California adults (21%) approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president (26% likely voters)—a record low across both terms of his presidency. For comparison, Donald Trump’s approval rating stood at 29 percent in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-1018.pdf). Today, overwhelming majorities of Democrats and independents disapprove of the president, while seven in ten Republicans approve.
Fewer approve of the way the US Congress is handling its job (16% adults, 17% likely voters). Two in ten or fewer have approved of Congress since June 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-june-2025/). Today, majorities across partisan groups disapprove of the US Congress.
Three in ten adults (30%) and about four in ten likely voters (38%) approve of the way their own representative to the US House of Representatives is handling the job. Shares are similar among Californians who currently live in a Democratic-held seat and a Republican-held seat. Four in ten or fewer across regions and demographic groups approve of the way their own House representative is handling the job.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (72%) disapprove of US military action against Iran. Most Democrats (94%) and independents (74%) disapprove, while about two in three Republicans approve (65%). About two in three or more across regions and demographic groups disapprove. California adults are more likely than adults nationwide (61%) to disapprove, according to an October Reuters/Ipsos (https://www.ipsos.com/sites/default/files/ct/news/documents/2026-10/Reuters%20Ipsos%20News%20Issue%20Survey%20October%202026%20Topline_3.pdf) poll.
Three in four adults (75%) and seven in ten likely voters (71%) disapprove of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing. Overall, seven in ten or more adults have disapproved since October 2025 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2025/). Today, most Democrats (95%) and independents (75%) disapprove, while most Republicans (72%) approve of ICE. Solid majorities across demographic and regional groups disapprove.
About two in three likely voters say they are very (25%) or somewhat (40%) confident that votes for Congress will be accurately counted nationwide. The share who are very confident has dropped from October 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2024/) (38%).

Methodology
The PPIC Statewide Survey has been conducted since April 1998 to provide a voice for the public, inform policymakers, encourage discussion, and raise awareness of critical issues facing California. The coauthors of this report include survey director Mark Baldassare, who holds the Miller Chair in Public Policy; associate survey director and research fellow Dean Bonner; survey analyst Lauren Mora, who was the project manager for this survey; and survey analyst Deja Thomas. The Californians and Their Government survey on state, local, and national issues is supported with funding from the Arjay R. and Frances F. Miller Foundation. The PPIC Statewide Survey invites input, comments, and suggestions from policy and public opinion experts and from its own advisory committee members, but survey methods, questions, and content are determined solely by PPIC’s survey team. We thank Paul Lewis and Eric McGhee for helpful reviews of an earlier report draft.
Findings in this report are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. The survey was conducted from October 16–22, 2026.
The survey was conducted by Ipsos, using its online KnowledgePanel, in English and Spanish according to respondents’ preferences. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability-based sampling and include both those with internet access and those without. KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and, if needed, a device to access the internet when they join the panel. KnowledgePanel members are primarily recruited using address-based sampling (ABS) methodology, which improves population coverage, particularly for hard-to-reach populations such as young adults and minority groups. ABS-recruited Latinos are supplemented with a dual-frame random digit dialing (RDD) sampling methodology that targets telephone exchanges associated with areas with a higher concentration of Latinos to provide the capability to conduct representative online surveys with Latinos, including those who speak only Spanish. KnowledgePanel’s recruitment was originally based on a national RDD frame and switched to the primarily ABS-based methodology in 2009. KnowledgePanel includes households with landlines and cell phones, including those with cell phones only and those without phones. ABS allows probability-based sampling of addresses from the US Postal Service’s Delivery Sequence File (DSF).
